prompt: A rural user on geostationary (GEO) satellite broadband says large downloads are fine but video calls feel laggy and web pages with many small requests are slow. The satellite is about 35,786 km up. What is the main explanation?

options.text: The satellite link has too little bandwidth for video
options.explanation: The user reports large downloads are fine, so capacity is not the main issue. The symptoms affect interactive, round-trip-heavy traffic.

options.text: Each round trip must travel up to the satellite and down twice, about 143,000 km, so propagation alone adds nearly half a second to every RTT
options.explanation: Correct. Four legs of about 36,000 km at the speed of light take about 477 ms, before slant range, processing and ground routing are added. Anything that waits for replies suffers; bulk transfers with large windows are less affected.

options.text: Radio signals travel much slower through space than through fibre
options.explanation: Signals in vacuum travel at the full speed of light, faster than in fibre. The problem is the enormous distance, not the speed.

options.text: Satellite links drop most packets, forcing constant retransmissions
options.explanation: Loss can occur, but the symptoms described (bulk fine, interactive slow) match high latency, which the altitude guarantees.

workedExample:
1. A bent-pipe satellite relays signals: request up and down, reply up and down, four legs in total.
2. At GEO altitude each leg is at least about 35,786 km, so a round trip covers about 143,000 km. At about 300,000 km/s that takes roughly 477 ms.
3. Slant range (you are rarely directly under the satellite), processing and terrestrial backhaul make the real RTT larger still.
4. Interactive traffic and protocols with many round trips (handshakes, chains of small requests) feel every one of those half-seconds; a large download, once flowing with a big enough window, mainly needs capacity.
5. Lower orbits (LEO) cut the propagation component dramatically, which is why LEO constellations target interactive use.

prompt: Over a very long distance, a route that goes up to low Earth orbit, across between satellites by laser, and back down can have lower propagation delay than a submarine fibre route between the same places, even though it travels further. Why?

options.text: Light travels about 47% faster in vacuum than in glass, and the extra distance up and down is small compared with a long intercontinental path
options.explanation: Correct. Fibre slows light to about 204,000 km/s against about 300,000 km/s in vacuum. Two extra legs of a few hundred kilometres matter little over, say, 17,000 km, but they dominate on short routes, where fibre wins.

options.text: Satellites have more bandwidth than fibre
options.explanation: Bandwidth does not set propagation delay. Fibre systems typically carry far more capacity than satellite links.

options.text: Laser links skip routing entirely, so there is no processing delay
options.explanation: Satellites and ground stations still switch and process traffic; the advantage is in propagation speed.

options.text: A space route is always faster than fibre, whatever the distance
options.explanation: On short routes the extra up-and-down legs outweigh the speed advantage, and real orbital geometry, hops and ground routing can erase it.

workedExample:
1. Propagation delay is distance divided by signal speed.
2. In fibre, light travels at about 204,000 km/s; in vacuum, about 300,000 km/s, roughly 47% faster.
3. A hypothetical 17,000 km route: fibre gives a round trip of about 167 ms. Going up 550 km, across 17,000 km and down 550 km (about 6% further) at vacuum speed gives about 121 ms.
4. Over a short route, though, the extra climb and descent dominate and fibre wins.
5. Real constellations add slant range, inter-satellite hop geometry, ground routing and processing, so no actual service advantage is guaranteed by this idealised comparison.
